title: Why Project Managers Inherit Scope Gaps They Did Not Create: A Prevention Guide
summary: Project managers absorb the cost of scope gaps written months before award. Here's how preconstruction decisions drive field disputes and how to break the cycle.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Scope gaps are written during pre-construction. Project managers pay for them in the field.
- The root causes are almost always the same: vague scope language, missed trade interfaces, and addenda that never reached the right sub.
- Field disputes follow predictable patterns. The trades and jobs that generate them are well-documented.
- Breaking the cycle requires change at the pre-con stage, not just better PM responses after the fact.
- Tools like[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) and[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) catch gaps before subcontracts are signed, so PMs inherit complete packages instead of problems.


You did not write the scope packages. You were not in the room when subcontracts were negotiated. But on bid day plus six months, you are the one standing in a trailer explaining to an owner why the electrical sub says conduit sleeves through the rated wall are not in their contract.


This is not bad luck. It is a structural problem in how pre-construction hands work off to operations. And in 2026, with nonresidential construction employment near its cycle peak and skilled crews harder to hold on to, the cost of a field dispute is not just a change order. It is schedule, crew morale, and sometimes the relationship with a sub you need on your next three jobs.


This guide explains where scope gaps come from, which ones show up most often in the field, and what your pre-con team can do differently so the next PM on the next project starts from a better position.


## Where Scope Gaps Actually Come From


Scope gaps are not random. They are produced by a small set of habits that repeat across bid, buyout, and field. The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , built from interviews with more than 200 general contractors, identifies a consistent pattern: the same gaps, the same trades, the same causes, project after project.


The most common root causes fall into four categories.


### 1. Vague or generic scope language


The phrase "as per plans and specs" appears in more scope packages than any other. It sounds complete. It is not. When a sub prices to their interpretation of "plans and specs," and you price to yours, the gap between those two readings becomes your change order.


A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC described the standard they aim for: "It's descriptive: bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"


That level of detail rarely makes it into a scope package assembled under bid-day pressure.


### 2. Trade interfaces nobody owns


The jobs that live between two scopes are the ones that fall through. The steel sub draws the embed. The concrete sub pours around it. Neither scope says who buys it or who sets it. The drawing shows the connection. The gap is in the contracts.


Provision's[Scope Gap Index](https://provision.com/scope-gap-index) , covering 1,290 scope packages across 24 projects in Q3 2026, found that anchors, embeds, and connections were flagged in 48% of all packages reviewed. That is 621 packages where this specific trade interface appeared unassigned.


Sealants and waterproofing joints were flagged in 45% of packages. Blocking and backing in 44%. These are not edge cases. They are the standard gaps.


### 3. Addenda that updated drawings but not scope packages


An addendum lands on day 12 of a 15-day bid period. The estimator updates the takeoff. The scope package does not get revised. The sub prices the original scope. You sign a subcontract based on a document set that no longer matches the drawings.


This is one of the most common sources of RFIs in the first 30 days of a project. The PM finds the conflict. The sub points to their scope. The GC absorbs the difference or fights for it.


### 4. Copy-paste from the last similar job


It is fast. It feels safe. And it imports every gap from the previous project into this one. The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) calls this out as one of the most reliable anti-patterns in pre-construction. The previous job had a different spec. A different structural system. Different subs with different baseline assumptions. The scope package that worked there does not work here.


## The Field Cost Is Real. The Dollar Examples Are Not Hypothetical.


The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) documents the dollar figures that operators have cited directly. These are not industry averages. They are specific gaps, on specific projects, described by the estimators and PMs who absorbed them.


- A $400K roof cover board missed on a $50M project. Recovered only through a relational concession from the sub.
- A $300K lead-lined glass omission on a hospital imaging suite. The GC absorbed it under "readily inferable" contract language.
- A $200K wood-flooring scope gap on a luxury condo. Not caught until buyout.
- A $45K stone-depth conflict between civil/structural and architectural drawings. Found at slab pour.


Arcadis puts the average construction dispute value in North America at $60.1M in their 2024 Global Construction Disputes Report. "Errors and omissions in contract documents" ranks as a leading dispute cause in North America. The dollar figures above show what that looks like at the project level.


A 2018 PlanGrid and FMI study estimated that miscommunication and bad project data drive $31.3B in annual U.S. rework. These are not abstract numbers. They show up as change orders on your cost report.


## Which Trades Generate the Most Field Disputes


Some trades are more gap-prone than others. That is not because their subs are less capable. It is because their work sits at more trade interfaces and involves more inferred scope.


The[trade-specific chapter of the Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) breaks these down in detail. The highest-frequency gap categories by trade include:


### MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing)


- Who sleeves and firestops the penetrations through rated walls
- Generator field conditioning costs (recurring across projects, described as "millions" by one operator)
- Motor starters: often specified but never assigned to a trade in the scope
- Lighting controls: drawn on electrical, specified in a separate controls section, priced by neither


Provision's Scope Gap Index found that anchors, embeds, and connections were flagged in 89% of electrical packages reviewed across 23 projects. Penetrations, sleeves, and firestopping appeared as a gap across masonry, concrete, and MEP divisions.


### Concrete and Steel


- Who sets base plate grout: not on the steel sub's standard scope, not on the concrete sub's either
- Concrete pumping: sometimes included, sometimes assumed, never explicit
- Embeds and anchor bolts at the steel-to-concrete interface


Anchors, embeds, and connections were the most-flagged item in the Metals division, appearing in 87% of 53 packages reviewed.


### Envelope and Roofing


- Roof cover board: often in the spec, rarely in anyone's scope
- Masonry-to-storefront flashings: where the two trades meet and the responsibility does not
- Caulking: interior versus exterior, different spec sections, different subs, one gap


Sealants, flashing, and waterproofing joints were flagged in 82% of Thermal and Moisture Protection packages in the Index.


### Drywall and Interior Finishes


- Wall blocking for future millwork, grab bars, or TV mounts: the drywall sub won't add it without an explicit scope item. The millwork sub assumes it's there.
- Gypcrete: the naming collision between self-leveling underlayment and gypsum board creates pricing confusion on nearly every multi-trade project.


## What Pre-Construction Gets Wrong at Handoff


The handoff from pre-construction to project management is where most of this information is lost. By the time a PM picks up the project, the bid assumptions have been summarized, the scope packages are signed, and the estimator has moved to the next pursuit.


Three things go wrong at handoff more than any others.


### The scope sheet and the subcontract say different things


A Director of Pre-Construction at a Mid-Market Southeast GC described the divide directly: "Pre-con is working in the scope sheet world and project management is working in the scopes of work." When those two documents conflict, the PM finds out in the field.


### Bid assumptions never become subcontract clarifications


During bidding, estimators make assumptions. Those assumptions should become explicit clarifications in the subcontract. Often they do not. The sub prices one thing. The GC assumes another. The PM inherits the gap.


### Addenda changes are not reflected in final scope packages


If the scope package was not updated after addenda, the PM is managing to a document that does not reflect the actual bid set. When the sub pushes back on a scope item, the PM cannot defend a scope package that predates the design change.


## What Better Pre-Construction Looks Like for PMs


The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) identifies eight habits that the best pre-construction teams use consistently. Several of them directly reduce what PMs inherit at project start.


### Drawings-first, not boilerplate-first


Scope packages built from the actual drawing set catch trade interfaces that boilerplate misses. When the scope starts from the drawings, the embed that does not appear on anyone's standard list gets included because it is on the structural drawings.


### Specific document references, not generic incorporation


Instead of "as per plans and specs," name the drawing. Name the spec section. Name the detail number. When a sub knows exactly which detail governs their scope, they price it. When they are told to interpret "plans and specs," they price the minimum.


### The pre-issue scope review checkpoint


One person reviews every scope package against the drawing set before it goes to subs. Not a five-minutes-before-bid review. A structured check, by trade, against the actual documents. This is where the missed firestopping gets caught. This is where the cover board goes into the roofing scope instead of becoming a change order six months later.


### Front-loading the buyout conversation


The best GCs start the scope conversation with subs before bid day, not after award. When a sub knows exactly what they are pricing, they price it correctly. When they find out at buyout that the GC expects them to include the grouting, the negotiation begins from a worse position for everyone.


As an Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC put it: "We have fewer subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope."

## Breaking the Cycle: What PMs Can Push For


Project managers often do not control what they inherit. But they can influence it. These are the asks that change what the next project looks like.


- **Ask for a scope package walkthrough at handoff.** Not a summary. Walk through the actual scope documents, trade by trade, and flag anything that looks ambiguous before subcontracts are signed.
- **Document the gaps you find.** When a field dispute traces back to a scope gap, write down what it was and where it came from. That data is the business case for better pre-construction process on the next bid.
- **Push for addenda reconciliation.** Ask pre-con to confirm that scope packages reflect the final addendum set before buyout closes. One question saves a lot of trailers conversations.
- **Use the first 30 days.** Walk scope with subs during early mobilization. Identify the grey areas before work starts. A clarification in week two is a conversation. The same clarification in week twelve is a change order.


The goal is not to do pre-construction's job from the field. The goal is to close the information gap that causes disputes before the first crew arrives on site.


For a deeper look at the scope language patterns that drive the most field disputes, the[subcontract language chapter of the Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/subcontract-language-scope) covers the specific contract clauses and scope formats that protect GCs and those that do not. It is worth a read before your next buyout.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Why do project managers absorb scope gaps they did not create?


Scope gaps are locked in during pre-construction, often weeks or months before a PM is assigned. By the time construction starts, subcontracts are signed and scope packages are fixed. The PM discovers the gap in the field, where the only options are negotiation, a change order, or absorbing the cost.


### What are the most common trades involved in scope gap field disputes?


MEP trades generate the most disputes, particularly around penetrations, firestopping, motor starters, and generator conditioning. Concrete and steel conflicts appear at embed and anchor interfaces. Envelope disputes involve cover board, flashings, and sealants. All of these appear as top-flagged items in Provision's Scope Gap Index across 1,290 packages reviewed in Q3 2026.


### How does vague scope language create field disputes?


Phrases like "as per plans and specs" allow subs to price their own interpretation. When the GC's interpretation differs, the gap becomes a change order. Specific scope language names the drawing, the spec section, and the trade responsible. That specificity eliminates the ambiguity that drives disputes.


### What is a subcontract scope dispute and how do PMs resolve it?


A subcontract scope dispute occurs when a sub and GC disagree about what a subcontract requires. Resolution usually means negotiation, a formal change order, or reviewing the original scope package and bid documents. When the scope package is vague, the GC is in a weaker position. Clear, source-traced scope packages reduce that exposure before the dispute starts.


### Can pre-construction software reduce the number of field disputes a PM inherits?


Yes. Tools like[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) generate trade-specific scope packages from the full drawing and spec set, with every item traced to its source. This catches trade interface gaps and addenda conflicts before subcontracts are signed. Provision's Scope Agent flagged at least one gap in 93% of 1,290 scope packages reviewed in Q3 2026.


### What should a PM ask for at pre-construction handoff to reduce scope disputes?


Ask for a trade-by-trade scope walkthrough before subcontracts close. Confirm that scope packages reflect the final addendum set. Flag any items that look ambiguous or unassigned. These questions take less than an hour at handoff and can prevent multiple change orders over the life of the project.


### What is "readily inferable" scope language and why does it hurt PMs?


"Readily inferable" is contract language that requires subs to include work that any experienced contractor would know is necessary, even if the drawings do not call it out explicitly. GCs use it to close scope gaps. Subs use it as a reason to exclude work they did not price. When it ends up in a field dispute, the PM is in the middle. The $300K lead-lined glass omission described in the Scope Gap Playbook was absorbed under exactly this language.
